bloques.titulo: What you will learn this week

bloques.html:
• Find the main ideas of an informational text and say how the text is organized.
  • Work out a writer's purpose, and spot bias.
  • Separate facts, opinions and reasoned opinions.
  • Put together information from two texts on the same topic: where they agree and where they disagree.
  • Unlock academic words with Greek and Latin roots and with context clues.
  • Write an explanatory paragraph that uses information from two sources.

1. Main ideas and structure

A good informational text has two or more main ideas. A summary gives those ideas in your own words, with no small details and no opinions of yours.

Writers organize information in a few common ways. The signal words tell you which one.

Structure What it does Signal words
Chronological tells events in the order of time first, in 1970, later, since then
Cause and effect explains why something happens and what follows because, as a result, consequently, for this reason
Problem and solution presents a problem, then ways to solve it the problem is, one solution, to reduce, to solve
Compare and contrast shows how two things are alike and different both, unlike, whereas, in contrast, similarly

2. Purpose and bias

Writers write to inform, to explain, to persuade or to entertain. To find the purpose, ask: What does this writer want me to know, think or do when I finish reading?

Bias means leaning toward one side. A biased text is not necessarily false, and a biased writer can still make a fair point. Read it with these questions in mind:

  • Who is writing, and what do they gain or lose?
  • Are there loaded words, chosen to make something sound better or worse than it is? (a few turtles, so-called experts)
  • Does the writer attack people and not their ideas?
  • Does the writer say "everybody knows" or "obviously" where evidence should be?
  • Is the other side missing?

3. Fact, opinion, reasoned opinion

Type Test Example
Fact It can be checked and shown to be true or false. Sea otters eat sea urchins.
Opinion It is a judgment; people can disagree. Otters are the most charming animals on the coast.
Reasoned opinion An opinion plus a reason or evidence that supports it. Otters should be protected, because kelp forests return where otters live.

In school writing and in science, an opinion with no reason is worth very little. A reasoned opinion can be discussed.

4. Two texts, one topic

When you read two texts about the same thing, make a quick chart before you answer:

Text 1 Text 2
Who writes, and why?
Main ideas
Where do they agree?
Where do they disagree?

Word box — Roots and context clues

Many academic words are built from Greek and Latin parts. Learn the part once and you can unlock dozens of words.

Root Meaning Words Root Meaning Words
astro, aster star astronomy, asteroid photo light photograph, photosynthesis
tele far telescope, telephone scope look microscope, periscope
bio life biology, biography geo earth geology, geography
hydr, aqua water hydrate, aquarium therm heat thermometer, thermal
micro small microscope, microbe graph write, draw paragraph, autograph
noct night nocturnal lumin, luc light luminous, translucent
naut sailor nautical, astronaut phobia fear claustrophobia
spect, vis look, see inspect, visible -logy study of biology, geology

Context clues. When the roots do not help, the sentence around the word usually does. Look for a definition (kelp, a giant seaweed), an example, a contrast (unlike..., but...) or the logic of the sentence (what must the word mean for the sentence to make sense?). Then put your guess in place of the word and read the sentence again.

Vocabulary of the week

Word Meaning Word Meaning
bias a tendency to favor one side purpose the reason why a text was written
source a text or person that information comes from to summarize to give the main ideas briefly, in your own words
consequently as a result whereas but, in contrast (joins two different facts)
to reduce to make smaller or less artificial made by people, not natural
to shield to cover something in order to protect or block to dim to make a light less bright
kelp a giant seaweed that grows in cold seas sea urchin a small, round sea animal covered in spines
to release to set free harvest (verb) to collect a crop or catch

Read the two texts. The examples refer to them.

Text 1 — Guardians of the Kelp (magazine article; text created for this guide)

Along the Pacific coast of North America grow forests that no hiker will ever walk through. They are made of kelp, a giant seaweed that rises from the sea floor toward the light. Fish, crabs and seals shelter among its stems.

Kelp has an enemy: the sea urchin, a spiny animal that chews through the base of the plant. Sea urchins have an enemy of their own: the sea otter, which eats them in great numbers.

For this reason, what happened to the otters also happened to the forests. By the early 1900s, fur hunters had wiped out the sea otters of British Columbia. As a result, urchins multiplied, and in many places the kelp disappeared, leaving bare rock. Around 1970, otters from Alaska were released near Vancouver Island. Since then, their numbers have grown, and where otters have returned, kelp has often grown back.

Text 2 — Ask the People Who Work on the Water (opinion column by a shellfish harvester; fictional author, text created for this guide)

My family has dived for sea urchins and clams for three generations. Since the otters came back, my catch has fallen by half, because an otter eats the same shellfish that I sell. Scientists love to call the otter a hero. They do not have to pay my bills. Obviously, anyone who has never worked on the water has no right to an opinion. I do not want the otters gone. I want a plan that counts fishing families as part of the coast, too.

Example 1 (main ideas and summary). Summarize Text 1 in two sentences. → Main idea 1: otters protect kelp forests by eating urchins. Main idea 2: when otters were hunted the forests shrank, and when otters returned the forests recovered. Summary: Sea otters keep kelp forests alive because they eat the urchins that destroy kelp. When hunters removed the otters the kelp disappeared, and it has often grown back where otters were returned.

Example 2 (structure). How is the third paragraph of Text 1 organized? → Signal words: For this reason, As a result. One event produces the next (no otters → more urchins → no kelp). It is cause and effect. It also follows time order, but the links between the events are what matter.

Example 3 (purpose and bias). What is the purpose of Text 2? Is it biased? → The writer wants readers to support a plan that protects fishing families: the purpose is to persuade. Bias check: the writer loses money because of otters; "love to call the otter a hero" is loaded; "anyone who has never worked on the water has no right to an opinion" attacks people, and "Obviously" stands where evidence should be. The text is biased. However, the writer also makes a fair point: otters really do eat the shellfish that harvesters sell.

Example 4 (fact, opinion, reasoned opinion). → "My family has dived for sea urchins and clams for three generations": fact (it can be checked). "Anyone who has never worked on the water has no right to an opinion": opinion with no reason. "My catch has fallen by half, because an otter eats the same shellfish that I sell": a claim with a reason, so it can be discussed and checked.

Example 5 (two texts). On what do the texts agree, and on what do they disagree? → Agree: otters came back, and otters eat sea urchins. Disagree: Text 1 presents the return as good news for the coast; Text 2 presents it as a cost for people who harvest shellfish. Neither text says that the otters should be removed.

Example 6 (roots). What is a "hydrothermal" spring? → hydr = water, therm = heat: a spring of hot water.

Example 7 (context clue). What does "wiped out" mean in Text 1? → Logic: after it, urchins multiplied and otters had to be brought from Alaska. So the otters were gone: killed completely.

Example 8 (explanatory paragraph). Explain why sea otters matter. → Sea otters are small animals with a large effect on the coast. (topic sentence) According to Text 1, they eat sea urchins, which destroy kelp. Consequently, where otters live, kelp forests survive and shelter fish, crabs and seals. (facts from a source, linked) However, Text 2 points out that otters also eat the shellfish that some families sell. (the other source) For this reason, protecting otters works best when fishing families are part of the plan. (closing sentence)
Use Text 1 and Text 2.
Which sentence in Text 1 defines the word kelp? Which type of context clue is it?
How is the second paragraph of Text 1 organized? (a) chronological (b) a chain of who eats what (cause and effect) (c) problem and solution. Give one reason.
Write one fact from Text 1 that could be checked in an encyclopedia.
Why did the author of Text 1 begin with "forests that no hiker will ever walk through"?
In Text 2, find one sentence that attacks people and not their ideas.
"Scientists love to call the otter a hero." Which word is loaded, and what does the writer want you to feel about scientists?
Write one thing that Text 2 tells you and that Text 1 leaves out.

A classmate says: "Text 2 is biased, so everything in it is false." Explain in two sentences why your classmate is wrong.

Roots and context.
Use the root box. What do these words mean? (a) nocturnal (b) geothermal (c) microbiology (d) aquanaut
Invent a word for "fear of stars" and a word for "an instrument for looking at light".
"The harbor was deserted: not a boat, not a person, not even a gull." What does deserted mean? Which clue helped you?

Complete with consequently, however or whereas: (a) Otters were hunted for their fur. , they disappeared from the coast. (b) Text 1 praises the otters, Text 2 complains about them. (c) Otters eat urchins. , they also eat clams.

Writing.

Explain in 6 to 8 sentences how sea otters, sea urchins and kelp are connected, and why not everybody is happy that otters have returned. Use information from both texts and at least two linking words.

Challenge mission — Bias detective. Find a real advertisement, headline or product label at home (a cereal box will do). Write down: one fact it gives, one opinion it gives, and one loaded word. Then rewrite it in one neutral sentence, with no loaded words at all. Show both versions to an adult and ask which one they would trust more, and why. Bonus: who wrote the original, and what do they gain if you believe it?
1. "They are made of kelp, a giant seaweed that rises from the sea floor toward the light." It is a definition clue: the meaning comes right after the word.
1. (b). Each sentence gives a link in a chain: urchins eat kelp, and otters eat urchins. Nothing is placed in time and no problem is being solved yet.
1. For example: fur hunters wiped out the sea otters of British Columbia by the early 1900s; otters from Alaska were released near Vancouver Island around 1970; sea otters eat sea urchins.
1. To surprise the reader and create interest: a forest you cannot walk through makes you want to know what kind of forest it is.
1. "Obviously, anyone who has never worked on the water has no right to an opinion." (Also acceptable: "They do not have to pay my bills.")
1. "love" (also "hero"). The writer wants you to feel that scientists are sentimental and do not care about working people.
1. Otters eat shellfish that people harvest for a living, so their return has cost some families money.

1. Bias means the writer leans to one side; it does not mean the facts are false. The writer's point that otters eat the shellfish the writer sells is true and agrees with Text 1, which says that otters eat urchins.
1. (a) active at night (b) heated by the earth; about heat from inside the earth (c) the study of very small living things (d) a person who explores under water, literally a "water sailor".
1. For example: astrophobia; photoscope. Any correct combination of the roots is fine.
1. Empty, with nobody there. The clue is the list of examples after the colon.
1. (a) Consequently (b) whereas (c) However.

1. Check: a topic sentence; the chain otters → urchins → kelp explained correctly; the harvesters' problem from Text 2; at least two linking words; your own words, not copied sentences; a closing sentence.

Challenge mission: the adult checks that the fact can really be checked, that the opinion is a judgment, and that the neutral version has no loaded words left.
